overview: Illyrian is an ancient label with changing meanings, applied to different peoples of the western Balkans. It does not describe one kingdom throughout this map’s 1500 to 400 BCE interval. The huge outline also includes northern Pannonian communities whose identity cannot simply be assumed Illyrian. Regional examples below include clearly marked later Hellenistic towns.

periods.title: Regional Iron Age communities
periods.summary: Archaeology reveals varied communities across the western Balkans, without proving a single ethnic or political identity.

periods.title: Later cities and rulers
periods.summary: Hellenistic towns and kingdoms developed; Rome defeated King Genthios in 168 BCE.

sections.title: Riverside households in the wider region

items.text: At Donja Dolina on the Sava, Iron Age builders raised timber houses on strong oak piles. Platforms supported rooms, sometimes with porches, and walkways connected neighboring buildings. These northern communities offer a regional example of adapting a home to wet ground, not a standard house for every people called Illyrian.

Donja Dolina’s archaeological finds include fishhooks, floats and net weights. Alongside fishing, residents grew cereals and legumes and kept domestic animals. Rivers, fields and herds supplied different parts of household food: dinner depended on several kinds of work.

Pottery, metal tools and ornaments show craft production at Donja Dolina, whose position on the Sava supported exchange. The municipal archaeological history describes its early Iron Age growth into an important trading center. A riverside settlement connected people who lived well beyond walking distance.

sections.title: A bird on wheels and changing towns

items.text: A burial mound at Glasinac yielded a remarkable small wagon in 1880. The Natural History Museum in Vienna dates it around 800 BCE. Its makers assembled bronze components around iron axles, putting considerable technical skill into an object much smaller than a real cart.

The wagon carries a bird-shaped vessel with another bird forming its lid. Scholars interpret it as a ritual object, but its original story is not preserved. The object gives us a memorable image of religious imagination without supplying a readable explanation of the ceremony.

At Dimal in present-day Albania, occupation began in the Iron Age, but the city flourished especially from the fourth to first centuries BCE. Its early urban core occupied a strongly fortified hilltop. This later city belongs to a different phase from most of the atlas’s earlier interval.

Dimal expanded after Roman annexation in 205 BCE, adding a larger circuit of walls and public buildings. Conquest therefore did not produce the same immediate outcome everywhere. At this particular settlement, urban construction continued under the new political arrangement.

sections.title: Wine jars, public lettering and gatherings

items.text: Dimal’s excavators identified transport jars of types used for Italian wine, including Lamboglia 2 and Brindisi forms of the later second and early first centuries BCE. These containers suggest supplies arriving mainly from southern Italy. Pottery fragments can preserve the route of a drink long after the liquid has gone.

Writing sample: locally produced Hellenistic roof tiles bear “ΔΙΜΑΛΛΙΤΑΝ,” meaning “of the people of Dimal.” Third-century BCE examples helped identify the ancient city. The wording is Greek, an attested public language in the region; it is not a deciphered sentence in an Illyrian language.

At Rhizon, now Risan in Montenegro, researchers uncovered monumental buildings of the third century BCE. The complex had limestone floors, later replaced in one room with carefully selected pebbles. Excavators interpret the exceptional architecture as a palace, possibly associated with local kings; the ownership is an interpretation.

The Rhizon buildings had broad entrances closed by wooden doors. Excavators recovered fragments of large door-knockers, and one doorway had molded decoration and half-columns. Even a doorway could announce that a visitor was entering an unusually grand building.

At Bushati in Albania, a fourth-century BCE building stood at the end of a ceremonial approach and monumental stair. The excavators interpret it as a hall for communal religious or civic meals. It provides evidence for organized gatherings, although the report cannot give us the guests’ actual conversations or menu.

King Genthios issued bronze coins using types already familiar at Shkodra and Lissos. He allied with the Macedonian king Perseus and was defeated by Rome at Shkodra in 168 BCE. The numismatic study connects his minting with military expenses, showing how war could affect the money people encountered.

ending.text: Roman expansion ended particular kingdoms and changed regional institutions over time. Genthios’s defeat in 168 BCE was one major event, not the disappearance of all western Balkan peoples. Dimal continued and later suffered destruction near the end of the first century BCE. The map’s 400 BCE endpoint is not a general cultural ending.
